title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 31–32
description: Advanced plant-based metaphors for causes, growth and decline, followed by precise vocabulary for animal classification, behaviour, habitats and animal welfare.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied textbook. Vocabulary teaching targets were checked against its unit pages, exercise pages and answer key; translations, explanations and example sentences are independently authored and no original extended texts, exercise prompts or illustrations are reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 31 sections A–B, diagrams, plant metaphors, exercises 31.1–31.6 and their answer key; Unit 32 sections A–D, Language help, exercises 32.1–32.5 including the word-family table, and their answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied selectively when confidently established for short targets. Empty IPA means the transcription was not sufficiently established; longer phrases may intentionally omit IPA. No live pronunciation audio was evaluated.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing material is in English except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations in the pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the PDF teaching pages, illustrations, exercises and corresponding answer key. Independently wrote examples and notes; programmatically validated JSON syntax, reference schema, IDs, metadata, provenance, and static Word/Sentence TTS target readability. Browser import, real TTS voices and speech recognition were not tested.
audit.limitations: No MP3 recordings are included. Live VocabLab importing and browser TTS/speech recognition remain untested. Animal-related words may have specialised scientific meanings beyond the textbook introduction.

units.title: Unit 31 — Taking root and reaping rewards
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 31. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Metaphorical language · plants, growth and decline
learningObjectives: Describe the beginnings, origins and consolidation of ideas using seeds, roots, stems and branches.
Use plant and gardening metaphors for excluding, limiting, discovering, succeeding and facing consequences.
Distinguish metaphors for flourishing from those for fading, shrivelling, wilting and withering.
Use fixed collocations such as nip it in the bud, thrive on challenges and the green shoots of recovery.

sectionsChecked: A and B teaching sections, explanations and illustrated vocabulary

items.example: The sudden rent increase sowed the seeds of discontent among the tenants.
items.note: Seeds metaphorically mark the beginning of an emotion or later development.

items.example: The pilot project planted the seeds of success for a much larger programme.
items.note: The image emphasises an early action from which later success may develop.

items.pt: plantar as sementes; dar início a algo
items.example: A series of small compromises sowed the seeds of a lasting agreement.
items.note: Figurative use of sow: set in motion a future outcome, positive or negative.

items.example: Researchers traced the roots of the ceremony to a local harvest festival.
items.note: Roots refers to the history or origins of a custom, idea or practice.

items.example: Poor communication turned out to be the root of the problem.
items.note: Identifies the underlying cause rather than a visible symptom.

items.example: After living abroad for a decade, she wanted to get back to her roots.
items.note: Often refers to returning to family, cultural or geographical origins.

items.example: They finally put down roots in a small coastal town.
items.note: Means to settle somewhere and establish a stable home or community.

items.example: The proposal initially met resistance but slowly began to take root.
items.note: An idea, belief or practice becomes established or widely accepted.

items.pt: apoiadores da base; militantes de base
items.example: Grassroots supporters helped organise the campaign in small communities.
items.note: Grassroots contrasts ordinary members with the leadership of a movement or organisation.

items.example: These assumptions are deeply rooted in the institution's history.
items.note: Commonly followed by in; can describe traditions, prejudice or beliefs.

items.example: The organisation's guiding values are firmly rooted in public service.
items.note: Firmly rooted in stresses a solid and enduring basis.

items.example: The disagreement stemmed from conflicting interpretations of the contract.
items.note: Stem from introduces a cause or origin; do not confuse it with stem an increase.

items.pt: cortar o mal pela raiz; impedir algo no começo
items.example: The manager tried to nip the rumour in the bud before it spread.
items.note: Stop an undesirable development at a very early stage.

items.example: The exhibition showcased several budding designers.
items.note: Usually describes someone showing potential but not yet fully established.

items.example: Customers can collect their orders from the nearest branch of the business.
items.note: Branch refers to a local office or shop belonging to a larger organisation.

items.example: The publisher plans to branch out into educational podcasts.
items.note: Often followed by into when a business or person enters a new field.

items.example: The selection process is designed to weed out applications that lack evidence.
items.note: Means remove unwanted elements from a group; can sound harsh when applied to people.

items.example: Funding pressures forced the council to prune back its renovation plans.
items.note: Means reduce the extent or scope of something rather than remove it altogether.

items.pt: colher os frutos; receber os resultados positivos
items.example: After years of careful preparation, the team began to reap the rewards.
items.note: Usually suggests enjoying the benefits of earlier effort or investment.

items.pt: colher o que se planta; arcar com as consequências dos próprios atos
items.example: He ignored repeated warnings and eventually had to reap what he sowed.
items.note: A proverb-like expression, often warning of predictable negative consequences.

items.example: The investigative team dug up correspondence that had never been published.
items.note: Figuratively discover facts, especially hidden or forgotten information.

items.example: A new research idea began to germinate during the conference.
items.note: Can describe an idea in the earliest stage of development.

items.example: Independent cafés have sprouted up across the neighbourhood.
items.note: Often suggests many new things appearing relatively quickly.

items.example: Small community initiatives began to sprout after the public meeting.
items.note: Both a botanical verb and a metaphor for something beginning to appear.

items.example: The community theatre flourished once volunteers took over its management.
items.note: Describes healthy, successful growth rather than simply continuing to exist.

items.example: Economists cautiously welcomed the green shoots of recovery in local manufacturing.
items.note: A metaphor for the earliest signs of improvement, especially economic.

items.example: The business shed several unprofitable activities after the merger.
items.note: Shed can describe losing or discarding employees, jobs, worries or weight, depending on context.

items.pt: perder as inibições; deixar a timidez de lado
items.example: During the improvisation workshop, participants gradually shed their inhibitions.
items.note: A fixed natural collocation for becoming less inhibited or self-conscious.

items.pt: cortar postos de trabalho; eliminar empregos
items.example: The struggling manufacturer expects to shed jobs next year.
items.note: Formal or journalistic expression for reducing employment; not the same as hiring.

items.example: The small research group thrived despite limited resources.
items.note: Means grow or develop successfully in particular conditions.

items.pt: dar-se muito bem com; prosperar sob determinadas condições
items.example: Some entrepreneurs thrive on the uncertainty of launching new ventures.
items.note: Thrive on introduces a challenge or condition that energises someone rather than overwhelms them.

items.example: Public enthusiasm began to fade as the delays continued.
items.note: Hopes, enthusiasm, memories and colours may all fade over time.

items.example: Rescue teams continued searching despite fading hopes of finding survivors.
items.note: The adjective fading expresses a gradual loss of hope.

items.example: Donations shrivelled after the economic downturn.
items.note: Often used of profits, revenues and support that have become much smaller.

items.pt: murchar; perder as forças ou o ânimo
items.example: The candidates visibly wilted under the pressure of the questioning.
items.note: Metaphorically means lose energy or confidence under difficult conditions.

items.example: Without continuing investment, the programme gradually withered.
items.note: More literary than fade when referring to the gradual loss of strength or vitality.

items.pt: um olhar fulminante; um olhar de profundo desprezo
items.example: She gave the speaker a withering look after his dismissive remark.
items.note: Withering describes a scornful look or remark that makes its target feel small.

items.pt: um comentário mordaz; uma crítica devastadora
items.example: The reviewer ended the article with a withering remark about the production.
items.note: A sharp, contemptuous comment; related to the metaphorical verb wither.

units.title: Unit 32 — The animal kingdom
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 32. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Nature · animal classification, behaviour and conservation
learningObjectives: Distinguish mammal, marsupial, rodent, reptile, carnivore, herbivore, predator and scavenger.
Contrast docile, tame, domesticated, wild, fierce and savage accurately.
Discuss migration, habitats, extinction, animal shelters, protected reserves and wildlife trade.
Use animal-related word families such as predator–predatory–prey on and migration–migrate–migratory.

sectionsChecked: A–D teaching sections, definitions and Language help

items.example: The whale is a mammal despite spending its entire life in the sea.
items.note: The unit contrasts mammals with fish and reptiles; the standard defining feature is feeding young with milk.

items.example: The zoologist observed a marsupial carrying its young in a pouch.
items.note: A subgroup of mammals whose young continue developing in a pouch.

items.example: The joey remained inside its mother's pouch for protection.
items.note: Here pouch means the body pocket in which a marsupial carries its young.

items.example: Several rodent species have adapted remarkably well to urban environments.
items.note: Category including mice, rats and squirrels.

items.example: The nature centre houses a collection of native reptile species.
items.note: Examples include lizards, snakes and crocodiles.

items.pt: carnívoro; animal que se alimenta de carne
items.example: This carnivore relies on smaller mammals for most of its diet.
items.note: Animal whose diet consists mainly or entirely of meat; not identical to predator.

items.pt: herbívoro; animal que se alimenta de plantas
items.example: An efficient digestive system enables this herbivore to eat tough grasses.
items.note: Animal whose diet is predominantly plant material.

items.example: The return of a major predator changed the behaviour of smaller animals.
items.note: A predator hunts other animals; the emphasis is on hunting, not merely diet.

items.pt: animal necrófago; animal que se alimenta de carcaças
items.example: As a scavenger, the bird often feeds on animals killed by other species.
items.note: Scavengers mainly feed on dead animals they did not kill themselves.

items.pt: de sangue quente; de temperatura corporal regulada
items.example: Birds are warm-blooded even though they are not mammals.
items.note: The unit contrasts animals maintaining their body temperature with those relying more on external heat.

items.pt: de sangue frio; dependente do calor ambiental
items.example: The cold-blooded lizard basked on a rock before becoming active.
items.note: A useful contrast with warm-blooded; the same phrase can describe a cruel human metaphorically.

items.example: Despite its size, the animal was remarkably docile around the keepers.
items.note: Emphasises gentle, easily managed behaviour, not necessarily training.

items.example: The tame fox approached visitors without showing any fear.
items.note: Tame means accustomed to people; a tame wild animal is not necessarily a domesticated species.

items.pt: domesticado; criado para conviver com humanos
items.example: Domesticated animals have lived alongside humans for countless generations.
items.note: Refers to a species bred or kept by people over many generations; unlike a single tame animal.

items.example: The biologists monitored a wild population rather than animals in captivity.
items.note: Opposite of domesticated in this context; not necessarily violent.

items.example: The story describes a savage animal attacking livestock.
items.note: Strongly negative word for violent or wild behaviour; avoid applying it carelessly to people.

items.example: A fierce dog kept strangers away from the farm entrance.
items.note: Describes aggressive, threatening behaviour; it can also describe intensity in other contexts.

items.example: Road construction has fragmented the fox's natural habitat.
items.note: The place where a species naturally lives and breeds.

items.pt: habitat em redução; habitat cada vez menor
items.example: Conservation groups are concerned about the bird's shrinking habitat.
items.note: A habitat becoming smaller through human activity or environmental change.

items.example: The birds migrate south before winter sets in.
items.note: Animals move from one region to another, often seasonally, to find suitable conditions.

items.example: Satellite tracking has revealed an unexpected migration route.
items.note: Noun from migrate; the unit highlights long-distance animal movements.

items.example: The researchers recorded the birds' complete round trip across the ocean.
items.note: The combined journey out and back; not a one-way trip.

items.example: Several island species became extinct after new predators arrived.
items.note: Extinct means no living members of a species remain; not merely endangered.

items.example: The conservation programme focuses on a rare flightless bird.
items.note: Used for birds that cannot fly.

items.pt: reserva de animais selvagens; reserva de caça
items.example: Visitors watched elephants at a game reserve under strict conservation rules.
items.note: Game can denote wild animals historically hunted; a reserve protects animals and may regulate access.

items.example: A guided safari in the game park offered excellent wildlife viewing.
items.note: An area where wild animals can be observed, usually with protection or management.

items.pt: santuário de aves; área protegida para aves
items.example: Volunteers restored nesting sites in the coastal bird sanctuary.
items.note: A protected place where birds can live and breed.

items.pt: animal perdido ou sem lar; de rua
items.example: The shelter arranged veterinary care for a stray dog.
items.note: As an adjective, describes a domestic animal that has wandered away or has no home.

items.example: They adopted their elderly cat from an animal rescue shelter.
items.note: A centre that cares for animals needing homes; distinct from a wildlife reserve.

items.example: Museum visitors learned why the dodo disappeared centuries ago.
items.note: A flightless bird that became extinct; the unit also notes a figurative sense.

items.pt: pessoa ultrapassada; pessoa desconectada do mundo atual
items.example: He called the outdated policy a dodo from another era.
items.note: Figurative, slightly mocking use for someone or something obsolete or out of touch.

items.pt: esportes envolvendo ferimento ou morte de animais
items.example: The charity campaigns for stricter restrictions on blood sports.
items.note: Activities pursued for entertainment that involve injuring or killing animals.

items.pt: o comércio de peles de animais
items.example: Campaigners challenged the ethical practices of the fur trade.
items.note: Industry that buys and sells animal fur, especially for clothing.

items.example: Rangers discovered traps left by a poacher near the reserve.
items.note: A person who catches or kills protected wildlife illegally.

items.example: The suspects were arrested for trying to poach endangered animals.
items.note: Verb corresponding to poacher; can also mean cook food gently in liquid, a different sense.

items.example: International agreements have restricted parts of the ivory trade.
items.note: Refers to buying and selling ivory, notably from elephant tusks.

items.example: An animal rights activist spoke at the public hearing about laboratory testing.
items.note: Someone who actively campaigns for protections and rights for animals.

items.example: The elephant's tusks were examined by the veterinary team.
items.note: Long projecting tooth, distinct from a horn.

items.example: Poachers targeted the rhinoceros for its horn.
items.note: A hard projection on an animal's head; distinct in structure from an elephant's tusk.

items.example: Although it looks harmless, the plant is carnivorous.
items.note: Adjective derived from carnivore; describes an organism that eats animal matter.

items.example: The herbivorous species relies on grasses throughout the year.
items.note: Adjective derived from herbivore.

items.example: The species developed a distinctive predatory hunting strategy.
items.note: Adjective from predator; metaphorically, can describe exploitative conduct.

items.example: These birds prey on small mammals at dusk.
items.note: In biology it means hunt and eat; figuratively it can mean exploit vulnerable people.

items.example: The wetland is an important stopping point for migratory birds.
items.note: Adjective from migration and migrate.

items.example: Humans began to domesticate different animal species thousands of years ago.
items.note: Verb linked to domestication and domesticated.

items.example: The domestication of livestock transformed early farming societies.
items.note: Noun for the process of adapting species to living with humans.
